title: Possessive Words Before Nouns
summary: Use my, our, your, his, her, their and its before nouns to show a relationship or who something belongs to. Keep its (possessive) separate from it’s (it is).
learningObjectives: Match I, we, you, he, she, they and it with my, our, your, his, her, their and its.
Put a possessive determiner before the noun it describes.
Choose his, her or their according to the person or people who possess or are related to something.
Distinguish the possessive determiner its from the contraction it’s meaning it is.

explanation.heading: Who does it belong to?
explanation.body: Use a possessive determiner before a noun to show ownership or a close relationship. The forms are I–my, we–our, you–your, he–his, she–her, they–their and it–its. The person or thing we talk about decides the possessive word.
explanation.example: We keep our bicycles beside the house.

explanation.heading: A noun follows the possessive word
explanation.body: Possessive determiners introduce a noun: my coat, your friends, his room or their bags. Do not use an object pronoun such as me or him in their place. Possessive words are used with plural nouns too: her books, our shoes.
explanation.example: Please write your name on the form.

explanation.heading: His, her and their show different relationships
explanation.body: Use his for a man or boy, her for a woman or girl, and their for two or more people. For one person, the same form works for possessions and family relationships, such as her phone and her brother.
explanation.example: Leo and Clara are visiting their grandparents.

explanation.heading: Its is not it’s
explanation.body: Its, without an apostrophe, means belonging to or associated with it. It’s, with an apostrophe, is the short form of it is. Check whether you could say it is: if you can, write it’s; if you mean belonging to it, write its.
explanation.example: The bird is sitting in its nest. It’s very quiet.

comparisons.title: A person versus something related to that person

left.label: Subject: she
left.note: She is the person doing the action.

right.label: Possessive: her
right.example: Her book is on the table.
right.note: Her comes before the noun book.

comparisons.title: Its without an apostrophe versus it’s

left.label: Possessive: its
left.example: The café has changed its menu.
left.note: Its describes the menu belonging to the café.

examples.sentence: My sister keeps her drawings in a folder.
examples.note: My refers to the speaker; her refers to the sister.

examples.sentence: You left your water bottle on the bench.
examples.note: Your describes the bottle related to you.

examples.sentence: We invited our cousins to dinner.
examples.note: Our shows the cousins are related to us.

examples.sentence: The children put their coats on the hooks.
The clock has stopped because its battery is flat.
examples.note: Its is possessive and has no apostrophe.

commonMistakes.why: Before the noun gloves, use the possessive my, not the object pronoun me.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Daniel forgot her coat at school.
commonMistakes.correct: Daniel forgot his coat at school.
commonMistakes.why: For Daniel, use his before the noun coat.
Use its without an apostrophe for the cat’s paws.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We told us neighbours about the party.
commonMistakes.correct: We told our neighbours about the party.
commonMistakes.why: Our is the possessive determiner that comes before neighbours.

studyTips: Learn subject and possessive pairs aloud: I–my, she–her, he–his, they–their.
Always connect the possessive word with its noun: our flat, your phone, his shoes.
Replace it’s with it is as a check: if the sentence stops making sense, you may need its.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Amir put ___ glasses on the kitchen table.
exercises.feedback: His is the possessive word used before glasses for Amir.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Nina and I share a garden. ___ garden has three trees.
exercises.feedback: Nina and I means we, so use our before garden.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: The dog followed ___ owner into the park.
exercises.feedback: Its is the possessive determiner for the dog; it’s means it is.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Can you and Mia bring ___ tickets tomorrow?
exercises.feedback: Your describes the tickets of the people being addressed.

exercises.prompt: Complete with a possessive word: I have a blue coat. ___ coat is on the chair.
exercises.feedback: My comes before coat to show the coat belongs to the speaker.

exercises.prompt: Complete with a possessive word: Alina owns a cat. ___ cat likes sitting by the window.
exercises.feedback: Her shows that the cat belongs to Alina.

exercises.prompt: Complete with a possessive word: Daniel has a little brother. ___ brother is six years old.
exercises.feedback: Use his before brother when talking about Daniel’s family.

exercises.prompt: Complete with a possessive word: The children have packed ___ own lunches for the school trip.
exercises.feedback: Their refers to the plural subject the children.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I cannot find me keys.
exercises.feedback: Use my, not me, to introduce the noun keys.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Sara is bringing she sister to the picnic.
acceptedAnswers: Sara is bringing her sister to the picnic.
exercises.feedback: Use her before sister, not the subject pronoun she.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The cat licked it's paws.
exercises.feedback: Its without an apostrophe shows the paws belong to the cat.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We invited we neighbours to the party.
acceptedAnswers: We invited our neighbours to the party.
exercises.feedback: The possessive word our comes before neighbours.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use a possessive word to restate “I have a green backpack.” Begin with “My backpack”.
speakingExercises.feedback: My is the possessive word for I and comes before backpack.

speakingExercises.prompt: Replace “Ella’s” with a possessive word: “Ella’s bicycle is red.”
speakingExercises.feedback: Her is used before bicycle for Ella.

speakingExercises.prompt: Replace the second mention of “the teachers” with a possessive word: “The teachers brought the teachers’ notebooks.”
speakingExercises.feedback: Their is the possessive word for the plural noun teachers.

speakingExercises.prompt: You and your brother share an apartment with one bedroom. Tell a friend about it in one complete sentence beginning 'Our apartment' and using the verb 'has'.
speakingExercises.feedback: Our comes before apartment because the apartment belongs to you and your brother together.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change 'She forgot her lunch.' into a sentence about Ben, a boy. Keep the action in the past tense, but change both pronouns correctly.
speakingExercises.feedback: He replaces she as the subject, and his replaces her before lunch for Ben.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend asks, 'Where is Mia's red helmet?' Reply in a complete sentence that the red helmet is under the desk. Replace 'Mia's' with a possessive word.
acceptedAnswers: Her red helmet is under the desk.
speakingExercises.feedback: Her is the possessive determiner for Mia and comes directly before red helmet.

speakingExercises.prompt: Maya and Zoe each brought a lunch. A friend says, 'Maya and Zoe brought her lunches.' Correct the possessive word and say the complete sentence.
acceptedAnswers: Maya and Zoe brought their lunches.
speakingExercises.feedback: Their refers to the two girls together and comes before the plural noun lunches.

speakingExercises.prompt: You and Ava share an apartment. Tell a new guest two short sentences: first, begin with 'This is' and say it is the apartment you share. Second, begin with 'Her' and say that Ava's room is upstairs.
acceptedAnswers: This is our apartment. Her room is upstairs.
speakingExercises.feedback: Our describes the shared apartment, while her describes Ava's room; both possessive words come before nouns.

listeningExercises.audioText: Omar forgot his raincoat, so he borrowed my umbrella.
listeningExercises.feedback: My refers to the speaker, whose umbrella Omar borrowed.

listeningExercises.audioText: The birds are feeding their chicks in the garden.
listeningExercises.feedback: Their refers to the birds, and chicks are the young birds they feed.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our neighbours planted flowers outside their house.
listeningExercises.prompt: Complete the expression you hear: “... outside ___ house.” Type one word.
listeningExercises.feedback: Their describes the house belonging to the neighbours.

listeningExercises.audioText: Marta brought her camera to the picnic, but she left my camera at home.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which of the two mentioned cameras did Marta take to the picnic?
listeningExercises.feedback: Her camera is Marta's, and she brought it. My camera belongs to the speaker and stayed at home.

listeningExercises.audioText: I can't find our seats. My brother has our tickets, so I'll ask him.
choices: A person working at the venue.
listeningExercises.feedback: Our means the tickets are shared, but the speaker's brother is the person holding them.

listeningExercises.audioText: The robot has lost its left wheel, but it's still moving slowly.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is happening to the robot?
choices: One wheel is missing, but the robot continues to move.
A different robot has stopped because it lost both wheels.
The robot has all its wheels and is standing still.
listeningExercises.feedback: Its refers to the robot's wheel, while it's means it is: the robot is still moving.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children's bikes are outside, but their helmets are inside.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words you hear immediately after 'but'.
listeningExercises.feedback: Their shows that the helmets belong to the children; the possessive word comes before helmets.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our neighbour will bring her guitar to the party tonight.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words you hear immediately after 'bring'.
listeningExercises.feedback: Her is a possessive determiner before guitar, referring to the neighbour.
